## Why does my baby cry so much — and what actually helps?

**TL;DR** — Long crying spells in a healthy young baby are very common, nobody fully knows what causes them, and they stop on their own by month three or four. The only treatment with reasonable evidence is a daily drop of friendly gut bacteria, and even that seems to help only breastfed babies.

### Start with what you can see

Every baby cries, but some healthy babies cry a shocking amount. The crying builds up over the first weeks, is worst around week six, and fades away by month three or four [Gutiérrez-Castrellón et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1097/md.0000000000009375). Doctors call the strong version colic, and the old rule for it is simple: crying at least three hours a day, on at least three days a week, for at least three weeks, in a baby who is otherwise healthy and growing well [Gutiérrez-Castrellón et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1097/md.0000000000009375). The newer rulebook keeps it even simpler: long crying with no clear reason, in a baby who is thriving [Benninga et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.016). Somewhere between one in twenty and one in five babies goes through this [Lucassen 2001](https://doi.org/10.1136/adc.84.5.398). And here is the part every tired parent should hear first: it is not linked to anything parents did — it hits boys and girls, rich and poor families, breastfed and bottle-fed babies alike [Lucassen 2001](https://doi.org/10.1136/adc.84.5.398).

### Why would a healthy baby cry like this?

The honest answer is that nobody knows for sure [Zeevenhooven et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41575-018-0008-7). The best clue points at the tummy. A baby's gut is home to huge numbers of tiny living things — gut bacteria — that help digest milk. Babies with colic often carry a different mix of these bacteria and show more signs of an irritated gut than babies without colic [Rhoads et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpeds.2018.07.042). In one study, the mix a baby started with even helped predict which babies would still be crying a month later [Loughman et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1017/s2040174420000227). There is a second clue that has nothing to do with tummies: children who were colicky babies grow up to get migraine headaches five to six times more often, so some colic might be an early form of pain instead of a gut problem [Gelfand et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1177/0333102414534326).

### So can we fix the mix?

That is the idea behind [probiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probiotic) drops — a daily drop of milk-friendly bacteria, given by spoon. When researchers pooled the four most careful tests, babies on the drops cried about twenty-five minutes less per day, and the benefit showed up in breastfed babies [Sung et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2017-1811). But now the twist. The biggest and strictest single test — 167 babies, including bottle-fed ones for the first time — found no help at all; if anything, the treated babies fussed a little more [Sung et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.g2107). Experts have settled in the middle: the drops are worth considering for breastfed babies with colic, and nothing is recommended for the rest [Szajewska et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1097/mpg.0000000000003633). The other things people buy mostly fail their tests: gas drops work no better than nothing [Ellwood et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-035405), special diets are backed only by weak studies [Gordon et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd011029.pub2), lactase drops make no clear difference [Kozłowska‐Jalowska et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1002/jpn3.12144), and spine or neck treatments stopped working the moment parents could not tell which babies got them [Dobson et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd004796.pub2). You can see the three big answers side by side in [Figure 1](#fig-colic-treatments).

### The part that matters most

The crying is genuinely hard on parents. Mothers dealing with long inconsolable crying had four times the odds of feeling depressed two months after the birth [Radesky et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2012-3316), and in one large survey about one parent in twenty admitted having shaken or slapped their baby because of the crying [Reijneveld et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736%2804%2917191-2). So the strongest medicine here is the plain truth: in every study that followed these babies, the crying faded by month three or four, with or without treatment [Hjern et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.15247). The children grow up fine — as teenagers they report a few more tummy complaints, but no lasting harm has been shown [Zeevenhooven et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.17215), [Indrio et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15030615). If you remember one line, make it this one: a healthy baby, terrible crying, nothing you did wrong — and it ends on its own around month three or four.

![Three horizontal lines with dots on one shared scale: the pooled drops trials sit left of the middle line, the biggest single trial sits right of it, lactase drops sit across it.](colic-treatments.png)

**Figure 1. The drops passed some tests and failed the biggest one.** Each line is one test's answer: the dot is its best guess, the line shows how unsure it was. Left of the middle means less crying than a fake treatment. The top test says the drops help, the middle says they do not, the bottom says lactase makes no clear difference [Sung et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2017-1811), [Sung et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.g2107), [Kozłowska‐Jalowska et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1002/jpn3.12144).
